UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


American Transmission Company LLC                                     Docket No. ER26-3531-000


                    MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF
                      AMERICAN TRANSMISSION COMPANY LLC

          Pursuant to Sections 212 and 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 1

American Transmission Company LLC by its corporate manager, ATC Management Inc.

(collectively, ATC) hereby files this Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer to the Comments

and Protests filed by the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (MISO) and Microsoft

Corporation (Microsoft). 2 On August 17, 2026, ATC filed its proposed revisions to Attachment

FF-ATCLLC of MISO’s Open Access Transmission, Energy and Operating Reserve Markets

Tariff (Tariff) in response to the Commission’s Show Cause Order. 3 In this Answer, ATC (1)

proposes modifications to its Attachment FF-ATCLLC in response to MISO’s operational

concerns, and (2) responds to other comments on ATC’s planning process, cost allocation and the

proposed template large load agreements. ATC’s proposed revisions address the immediate need

for large load integration in the ATC service territory and are just and reasonable and should be

accepted by the Commission without hearing or settlement proceedings with an effective date of

October 17, 2026.




1
    18 C.F.R. § 385.212-213 (2026).
2
 Comments and Protest of the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (MISO Protest) and
Protest of Microsoft Corporation (Microsoft Protest).
3
 Midcontinent Indep. System Op., Inc., Order Instituting Proceeding Under Section 206 of the Federal
Power Act, 195 FERC ¶ 61,212 (2026) (Show Cause Order).
 I.     SUMMARY OF ANSWER

       For nearly two decades, ATC has operated under its own local planning rules that are

incorporated in the MISO Tariff. Among other things, Attachment FF-ATCLLC currently

governs load interconnections to the ATC transmission system. ATC studies load interconnection

requests, determines what facilities are needed and then feeds the study results and proposed

transmission facilities to MISO for evaluation in the regional planning process for inclusion in

the MISO Transmission Expansion Plan (MTEP) through the regular annual process or the

Expedited Project Review (EPR) process. ATC’s Commission-approved local planning process

has worked without issue since it was approved. ATC’s proposed revisions to Attachment FF-

ATCLLC are intended to codify and reflect the processes that ATC follows today with respect to

managing the challenges of large load interconnections and other revisions that reflect new,

proposed practices to comply with the Show Cause Order.

       Since the Commission approved ATC’s transmission planning process in Attachment FF-

ATCLLC under Order No. 890, ATC has revised that process to comply with Order No. 1000 and

other transmission planning-related reforms issued by the Commission – all of which

complement MISO’s regional planning process. ATC’s proposed revisions in this docket are no

different: they update the local planning process per the Commission’s direction. In ATC’s view,

the Show Cause Order builds on the Commission’s previously approved local planning

framework by requiring updates to meet the specified requirements.

       ATC began receiving requests in 2023 from the Local Distribution Companies (LDCs)

connected to its transmission system requesting studies for large load interconnections. ATC

responded to concerns about cost allocation and transparency related to large loads by

developing the processes reflected in the proposed revisions to Attachment FF-ATCLLC. As the



                                                2
 Commission noted in the Show Cause Order, ATC’s Attachment FF-ATCLLC includes an

approved distribution-to-transmission interconnection process and a load interconnection

procedure, but it does not have procedures specific to large loads. 4 ATC’s proposed revisions in

this filing are intended to fill that gap and are tailored to work within the established Attachment

FF-ATCLLC procedures. In sum, ATC’s proposal here is intended to formalize what ATC is

already doing in its footprint to manage the challenges of large load integration and add new

practices that build upon ATC’s long-standing local planning processes.

         Nevertheless, ATC recognizes MISO’s need for regional visibility into, and operational

authority over, loads of 50 MW or more. As discussed below, ATC proposes targeted revisions to

Attachment FF-ATCLLC to address MISO’s concerns and eliminate any perceived operational

gaps. ATC will modify its Large Load definition threshold to 50 MW as follows:

         •   ATC’s large load criteria will apply within the ATC footprint. Large loads over 50

             MW connecting to ATC’s system will be required to comply with MISO’s IRR

             requirements when they become effective if ATC does not have applicable criteria on

             a given topic.

         •   ATC will modify Attachment FF-ATCLLC and any related business practices to

             ensure that ATC’s large load planning and interconnection criteria will apply to all

             Large Loads over 50 MW.

         •   For Large Loads over 50 MW, ATC will distinguish between computational loads and

             other large loads for power factor and other requirements as deemed necessary by ATC.

         For cost allocation purposes, ATC will maintain the 100 MW threshold for application of

ATC’s proposed Large Load Project Commitment Agreement (LLPCA) and Minimum


4
    Show Cause Order at P 21, n. 75.

                                                  3
 Transmission Charge Agreement (MTCA). The 100 MW threshold is important for cost

allocation purposes to coincide with the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin’s (PSCW)

established 100 MW threshold for large load tariffs to avoid stranded costs to ATC’s

interconnected LDCs. If ATC is required to lower its threshold to 50 MW for cost allocation

purposes, LDCs with large load tariffs in ATC’s footprint will be unable to directly assign the

large load upgrade costs to the particular large loads causing those costs to be incurred. As a

result, any upgrade costs for large loads between 50 and 100 MW would be spread to the LDC’s

other customers.

       If these modifications are acceptable, ATC requests that the Commission issue an order

accepting the Attachment FF-ATCLLC filing on the condition that ATC submit a compliance

filing implementing the proposed changes above within 30 days.

       The remainder of ATC’s Attachment FF-ATCLLC revisions should be accepted as just

and reasonable. ATC’s template large load agreements (LLPCAs and MTCAs) will be posted on

ATC’s website. While ATC is not requesting approval of these template agreements as pro forma

agreements, they nevertheless provide consistency and allow flexibility for large load customers.

As mentioned previously, Attachment FF-ATCLLC was developed and approved in a series of

planning orders, as meeting Order 890’s 5 transmission planning process and Order 1000’s

requirements. 6 ATC’s proposed changes are consistent with Order No. 890 principles. Finally,

there are no material issues of fact that warrant hearing and settlement procedures

 II.       MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

          To the extent required, ATC respectfully requests leave to submit this Answer. The

Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure prohibit answers to protests unless otherwise

authorized. 7 The Commission regularly allows answers for good cause shown, such as when the

answers help ensure a more accurate and complete record, clarify the issues, or provide useful

and relevant information that will assist the Commission in its deliberative process. 8 ATC’s

Answer will clarify the record and ensure a more accurate and complete record. Because this

information will assist the Commission in its decision-making, ATC respectfully requests that the

Commission accept this Answer for good cause shown.

III.      ANSWER

          A.      ATC’s Proposed Attachment FF-ATCLLC Revisions Address the Immediate
                  Need for Large Load Integration in ATC’s Footprint.

          ATC appreciates the potential complexity caused by the misalignment in the Show Cause

Order compliance schedules of ATC and MISO. MISO’s compliance processes are working their

way through the stakeholder process. Once filed, MISO’s proposed compliance filing could take

many months to finalize with follow-up compliance filings and potential challenges. Given that

transmission owners in the MISO Region have their own local planning process (even though

they are not included in the MISO Tariff), existing practices may vary greatly across the region.




P 36, on reh’g, 132 FERC ¶ 61,119, PP 20-22 (2010); Midwest Indep. Transmission Sys. Operator, Inc.,
123 FERC ¶ 61,165 (2008), order on reh’g, 127 FERC ¶ 61,169 (2009).
7
    18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2).
8

to answers “because they have provided information that assisted us in our decision-making process”);
Texas Eastern Transmission, LP, 122 FERC ¶ 61,205 at P 8 (2008) (accepting answer that completed the
record); California Indep. Operator Corp., 105 FERC ¶ 61,284 at P 10 (2003) (accepting ISO’s answer
that clarified the issues).

                                                   5
 Thus, any consensus proposal that MISO develops may necessarily be at a high level, with room

for individual variation. It could be well into 2027 before any MISO-wide large load rules are in

effect. ATC’s proposed revisions provide an immediately implementable path forward,

consistent with ATC’s current practices, offering certainty for large-load projects already

underway in ATC’s footprint and establishing urgently needed protections against cost shifting.

       ATC has already committed to adjusting its processes, if necessary, through its Business

Practices or otherwise, as MISO’s requirements develop through the stakeholder process. MISO

suggests that ATC should defer its proposal because it may conflict with MISO’s future

compliance filing. ATC is participating in the stakeholder process for developing MISO’s

region-wide Show Cause Order compliance filing and intends that ATC’s processes will continue

to work with MISO’s planning processes similar to how ATC’s Attachment FF-ATCLLC works

with MISO’s Attachment FF today. A direct conflict is even less likely after the changes ATC is

proposing in Section C, below. However, if a direct conflict arises, ATC will work with MISO to

resolve it. Implementing ATC’s revisions on October 17, 2026 will provide timely clarity and

certainty while advancing changes that are independently just and reasonable and responsive to

the Show Cause Order.

       B.      Uniform Rules Across the MISO Region May Be Unjust and Unreasonable if
               They Impose Unnecessary Burdens or Conflict with State Requirements.

       Consistent with Wisconsin state law, local planning is a core function of ATC’s

operations. ATC’s own robust local planning process has worked collaboratively within MISO’s

regional planning umbrella for nearly two decades. Nothing in ATC’s proposed changes to

Attachment FF-ATCLLC is intended to change that collaborative framework. For nearly three

years, ATC’s studies and reliability analyses have determined that the appropriate threshold for

categorizing large loads in ATC’s footprint should be 200 MW. That threshold has thus far not

                                                 6
 resulted in any reliability or instability issues to date. In light of the current development efforts

and the PSCW actions to date, ATC determined that 100 MW would strike the right balance

between state cost allocation determinations and maintaining system reliability in ATC’s

footprint.

          A single set of uniform rules for the entire MISO region 9 will necessarily have to reflect a

broadly applicable regional baseline, which could impose unduly burdensome requirements in

ATC’s footprint. Each new large load presents its own unique characteristics, and ATC’s system

is uniquely situated among the Great Lakes and the Mississippi River. Load interconnections are

dynamic and reliability issues can be highly technical; a one-size-fits-all approach can result in

unnecessarily onerous requirements and costly equipment specifications. ATC has confronted

the challenges posed by large loads, studied them, and developed workable, proven

requirements. ATC engaged specialized power system consultants to study large loads, including

flicker analyses, rotor-swing modes, generator-shaft studies to develop ramp-rate, oscillation,

and voltage-ride-through requirements. The Commission should give due weight to ATC’s

preparedness and should not disadvantage ATC for advancing proven large load processes

developed over the past several years and submitting them within the Show Cause Order’s

original timeframe.

          ATC disagrees with MISO’s assertion that ATC’s large load processes would produce

“unjust and unexpected outcomes” for large loads. Rather, requiring ATC to alter its existing

practices – particularly for large load projects already underway in its footprint – would itself

produce an unjust result. This does not mean that ATC’s processes will remain static. ATC has

continually reassessed them and will continue to do so in light of MISO’s forthcoming


9

                                                    7
 compliance filing and the new NERC Reliability Standards under development. No reliability

gaps will arise because the NERC Reliability Standards will soon apply to all large loads,

including those in ATC’s footprint.

           C.      ATC’s Proposed Modifications Will Address MISO’s Operational Concerns.

           MISO suggests there will be practical implementation problems if it is unclear how ATC's

separate application, study, and agreement processes would interface with MISO's own

transmission service and Large Load Section 205 filings currently in development. MISO asks

the Commission to direct ATC to file revised tariff sheets that “adopt or integrate with” MISO’s

large load rules and remove redundant processes.

           ATC recognizes MISO’s concerns and agrees to modify its Attachment FF-ATCLLC

proposal in certain respects to eliminate any perceived operational gaps that could arise for loads

between 50 and 100 MW. ATC will agree to modify its Large Load definition threshold to 50

MW for certain operational processes as follows:

           •    ATC’s large load criteria will apply within the ATC footprint. Large loads over 50

                MW connecting to ATC’s system will be required to comply with MISO’s IRR

                requirements when they become effective if ATC does not have applicable criteria on

                a given topic.

           •    ATC will modify Attachment FF-ATCLLC and any related business practices to

                ensure that ATC’s large load planning and interconnection criteria will apply to all

                Large Loads over 50 MW. As described above and in the filing letter, ATC’s planning

                and interconnection criteria is study-based and tailored to ATC’s footprint. 10 MISO’s

             proposed 50 MW threshold is based on the threshold suggested in the Show Cause

            Order and is not based on studies specific to the MISO region.

        •   For Large Loads over 50 MW, ATC will distinguish between computational loads and

            other large loads for power factor and other requirements as deemed necessary by

            ATC.

        If the Commission accepts these modifications, ATC requests that the Commission issue

an order accepting the Attachment FF-ATCLLC filing on the condition that ATC submit a

compliance filing with revised tariff sheets implementing the proposed changes above within 30

days.

        ATC’s proposed revisions to Attachment FF-ATCLLC describe processes that are

designed to work together with MISO’s process in the same way ATC’s local planning process in

Attachment FF-ATCLLC works with the annual MTEP process today. ATC’s application process

and studies of all distribution interconnections, including large load interconnections,

contemplates close coordination with MISO. ATC works closely with MISO to provide it with

all necessary information so that the interconnection can be integrated into the annual MTEP,

which may include on an as needed basis, review and approval on an expedited timeline through

MISO’s EPR process. Moreover, NERC’s new large load Reliability Standards will soon be

applicable to all large loads, including those in ATC’s footprint. Upon Commission acceptance

of these changes to Attachment FF-ATCLLC, ATC will continue to coordinate with MISO to

ensure all projects interconnecting to ATC’s system are included in MTEP either through the

standard planning process or the EPR process. 11

            D.       ATC’s 100 MW Threshold for Cost Allocation is Driven By a State-
                    Determined Threshold and Should Be Accepted.

           ATC proposes to maintain its 100 MW threshold for large loads for cost allocation

purposes. ATC’s threshold aligns with the PSCW's determination in separate retail proceedings

that 100 MW is the appropriate threshold for large load cost-shifting protections at the retail

level. 12 The PSCW made a finding of fact that it would be reasonable to make the large load

tariffs mandatory for all customers with an aggregate load forecast of 100 MW and therefore

ordered the large load tariff mandatory for all customers with an aggregated load forecast of over

100 MW. 13 If ATC is required to implement a 50 MW threshold for cost allocation purposes,

there will be a cost allocation gap at the state level. LDCs with those large load tariffs in

Wisconsin will be unable to directly assign costs to the large loads between 50 and 100 MW that

cause the network upgrade costs to be incurred. 14 Thus, network upgrade costs regarding loads

between 50 and 100 MW will be spread to the LDC’s other customers.

the benefit of all users of its Transmission Facilities.”).

        E.      Template LLPCAs and MTCAs Posted on ATC’s Website Provide
               Consistency and Allow Flexibility.

       ATC’s proposes to apply the 100 MW threshold for cost allocation purposes by requiring

that all large loads interconnected to ATC’s system execute the LLPCA and MTCA agreements. 15

These agreements deliver two layers of protection.

       First, during construction, the Amended LLPCAs require LDCs to (1) backstop the cost

of the required network upgrades in case the large load project is cancelled before it goes into

service and (2) pay the carrying costs for Construction Work in Progress (CWIP) that ATC would

otherwise recover from all of its transmission customers through its Attachment O formula rate.

These mechanisms protect against other ATC customers paying for stranded costs if the large

load projects are canceled before entering service.

       Once the facilities are placed into service, the MTCA requires LDCs to pay a minimum

contribution to ATC’s transmission revenue requirement based on the amount of transmission

capacity that the LDC requested to serve the large load. ATC proposes to roll-in the capital costs

of the network upgrades for large loads rather than directly assign them to LDCs. The MTCA

with its minimum transmission contribution will ensure the large load project costs are not

unreasonably shifted to other transmission customers in the event the large load does not

materialize to the extent requested. Moreover, the total charges incurred under the MTCA will

be limited to the incremental revenue requirement of the required network upgrades so that the

LDC does not overpay under the agreement. ATC’s proposed approach generally follows the




 ATC recently filed executed LLPCAs and an MTCA with Wisconsin Electric Power Company in
15

Docket No. ER26-3265, which is pending a Commission order.

                                                11
 Transmission Security Agreement framework the Commission has already accepted in other

proceedings without a hearing. 16

        ATC has a series of template agreements that will assist with large load interconnections.

First, ATC already employs standardized Distribution-Transmission Interconnection agreements

(D-TIAs) that are posted publicly and filed with the Commission when executed, serving the

same transparency function. In addition, proposed section VI.12.B of Attachment FF-ATCLLC

requires that LLPCA and MTCA templates 17 be posted on ATC's public website and filed with

FERC for acceptance upon execution. These template agreements achieve comparable

transparency and consistency to a pro forma agreement without foreclosing project-specific

adjustments that may be needed given the individualized nature of large load projects. Any

unreasonable variations in these agreements can be brought to the Commission’s attention via the

filing of an unexecuted agreement.

        F.      ATC’s Proposed Changes are Consistent with Order No. 890 Principles.

        ATC is the only transmission owner in MISO that codifies its local planning process in

the MISO Tariff and has received specific findings that those local processes are compliant with

Orders Nos. 890 and 2000. ATC’s planning processes are structured to include all interested

parties and treat all similarly situated interconnected customers the same. ATC's planning

process is open, collaborative, and stakeholder driven.

  The LLPCA protects transmission customers from the financing costs of construction and other costs
arising if a large load project is canceled before completion. The MTCA, with its Minimum Transmission
Charge, protects other transmission customers after the project is placed into service in the event the full
amount of the requested load does not materialize. Combined, the agreements protect other transmission
customers from unjust and unreasonable cost shifts that could occur if the large load fails to materialize.

            However, under Wisconsin law ATC's direct contractual and Tariff relationship is with

LDCs, not end-use retail customers. Because ATC is prohibited from providing transmission

service directly to retail customers, the local planning process necessarily is focused on the needs

of entities, such as LDCs, with distribution facilities connected to ATC’s system. 18 ATC does not

share information regarding interconnection requests from LDCs with third parties for

confidentiality reasons, much like in the generator interconnection context. It is up to the LDC

making an interconnection request to determine what information to share with its retail customer.

           ATC agrees with Microsoft’s contention that stakeholders should have the option to

participate in the local planning process, such as to test and validate local transmission needs,

explore solutions to challenges and support consideration of GETs. 19 Given the confidentiality

concerns mentioned above, such stakeholder participation does not occur in connection with a

particular interconnection request, but otherwise stakeholders have an ability to participate.

ATC’s network adequacy planning process is open to stakeholder engagement. As provided in

Attachment FF-ATC, ATC conducts an annual Ten-Year Assessment (TYA) “of the need to

modify, extend or construct new Transmission Facilities to provide, safe, reliable,

Interconnection Service and transmission Service and to ensure that its Transmission Facilities

are capable of providing and have the Physical Capacity and operating Capability to reliably

provide adequate transmission Service to meet the needs of all uses of its Transmission Facilities

        G.      There are No Material Issues of Fact that Warrant Hearing and Settlement
                Procedures.

        The Commission has discretion to direct an evidentiary hearing where there are genuine

issues of material fact that cannot be resolved on the written record. 28 Although protests

routinely identify disagreements in Section 205 proceedings, it is well established that “mere

conjecture does not create a genuine issue of material fact warranting a hearing.” 29 Any factual

dispute presented here—although none appears to exist—can be resolved on the written record.

        ATC has already agreed to modify the large load threshold regarding the operational

issues that MISO identified. ATC has also agreed to continue working with MISO to ensure that

its planning process works seamlessly with MISO’s processes as it does today. In addition,

potentially preventing proper cost allocation that protects other ratepayers from paying for

upgrades to ATC’s system caused by new large loads.

IV.      CONCLUSION

         For the foregoing reasons, ATC’s proposed revisions to Attachment FF-ATCLLC are just

and reasonable and will provide greater clarity and transparency for the immediate and reliable

interconnection of large loads in ATC’s footprint. ATC respectfully requests that the

Commission grant leave to answer, accept this Answer, deny the requests for hearing and

settlement judge procedures, and accept the Amended LLPCAs and the MTCA as just and

reasonable, effective October 17, 2026 (60 days from the date of filing).
